zh: 先数出每台服务缓存的请求数 c[i]。如果能在时间 T 内完成，那么更长的时间也一定能完成，所以可以二分答案 T。
固定 T 时：c[i]>T 的服务至少要把 c[i]−T 个请求交给别人；c[i]≤T 的服务做完自己的请求后，剩余时间还能接收 ⌊(T−c[i])/2⌋ 个外来请求（每个耗时 2）。只要总接收容量不小于总外包量就可行。
在 [0, max(c)] 上二分：对每个 mid，累加 excess=Σmax(0,c[i]−mid) 和 capacity=Σ⌊(mid−c[i])/2⌋（只对 c[i]≤mid 的服务，并且每台单独向下取整，不能合并零碎时间）；capacity≥excess 则 high=mid，否则 low=mid+1。输出 low，累加量用 64 位整数。
en: First count the cached requests c[i] of each service. If everything can be finished within time T, it can also be finished within any longer time, so binary search the answer T.

For a fixed T: a service with c[i] > T must hand off at least c[i] - T requests; a service with c[i] <= T, after finishing its own requests, can still accept floor((T - c[i]) / 2) foreign requests, each taking 2. T is feasible as long as the total accepting capacity is at least the total handed off.

Binary search over [0, max(c)]. For each mid, accumulate excess = sum of max(0, c[i] - mid) and capacity = sum of floor((mid - c[i]) / 2) over services with c[i] <= mid, flooring each service separately (leftover fragments of different services cannot be combined). If capacity >= excess set high = mid, otherwise low = mid + 1. Output low, and accumulate in 64-bit integers.

explanationEn:
## Fixed source and disclosure of corrections

The original rules come from fastprep/Thoughtspot/thoughtspot-get-min-time.md at fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc: each request takes 1 on its cache service and 2 on any other service; different services work in parallel, and one service handles only one request at a time; all requests are assigned freely to minimize the time at which everything is finished. The catalog truncated the HTML at 1<=i<=m, swallowing the key 1/2 costs and the parallelism rule. The original text has no extra arrival times, dependencies, or requirement to keep the input order.

The Constraints section of the raw text indeed says Unknown and gives no numeric bounds. The complete input envelope comes from web/content/docs/companies/thoughtspot.mdx of the same fixed commit: 1 <= n, m <= 100000 and 1 <= cache[i] <= n. This site records the two sources separately, does not pretend these bounds come from the raw text, and does not shrink the MDX ranges. The standard input/output was compiled by this site; the original example is kept, and two more public examples are this site's additions. Upstream code was not executed.

The answer 3 of the original example n = 3, cache = [1,1,3,1,1] is correct, but its explanation assigns the 3rd request to service 2 and says it takes 1, which contradicts its cache service 3. A correct assignment achieving the same answer is: service 1 handles requests 1, 2 and 4, service 3 handles request 3, and service 2 handles request 5, taking 3, 1 and 2 respectively. The compiled solution only returns the maximum cache frequency 4, ignoring that non-cache services can also execute requests; this site does not adopt that wrong algorithm.

## Approach

Count each service's cached requests c[i]. Binary search the candidate finishing time T: a service with more than T cached requests must hand off at least c[i] - T of them; a service with fewer than T can first finish its own c[i] requests and then accept floor((T - c[i]) / 2) other requests. Compute the total handed-off amount E and the total accepting capacity C; T is feasible when C >= E. The upper end of the range is max(c), because executing everything on its cache service is always feasible. Note that each service's remaining time must be floored separately; leftover fragments of different services cannot be combined.

## Proof of correctness

Necessity: consider any assignment that finishes within T. Service i handles x[i] of its own cached requests and y[i] non-local requests, so x[i] + 2y[i] <= T and x[i] <= min(c[i], T). It handles at most x[i] + floor((T - x[i]) / 2) requests. The function x + floor((T - x) / 2) is non-decreasing in the integer x, so the service's total is at most min(c[i], T) + floor((T - min(c[i], T)) / 2). Summing over all services, finishing all m requests requires m <= sum of min(c[i], T) + C, which is equivalent to E <= C.

Sufficiency: let every service first handle min(c[i], T) of its own requests; exactly E requests are left over. Only services with c[i] > T produce handed-off requests, and only services with c[i] < T have accepting capacity, so an accepting service can never be the original cache service of these requests, and each handed-off request indeed takes 2. Every handed-off request can go to any service with capacity, so if C >= E they can all be assigned without any service exceeding T. Therefore the capacity criterion is necessary and sufficient.

If T is feasible, increasing the time does not invalidate the assignment, so feasibility is monotone. The binary search returns the smallest feasible integer T, i.e. the minimum finishing time. All task durations are integers and there are no arrival constraints, so a fixed assignment executed back to back in any order finishes at the sum of that service's task durations; the integer time model misses no better schedule.

## Complexity

Counting is O(m + n), the binary search O(n log(m + 1)), and the space O(n + m) (including parsing the input). The full n = m = 100000 runs directly with no special case for native languages; the answer is at most m. Even if the intermediate capacity total reaches n * m, 64-bit integers should be used; Python integers are safe.

## Independent verification

A small oracle enumerates directly which service each request is assigned to, adds 1 to that service's load when the cache matches and 2 otherwise, and takes the minimum over all assignments of the maximum load; it uses neither the capacity criterion nor binary search. 163 unique inputs were cross-checked through real subprocesses. The official cases cover odd idle times, idle services, all requests concentrated, and the full n/m bounds. At full scale, a single service gives 100000; 100000 services with one request each give 1; 100000 services with all requests on one cache give 2; only two services with 100000 concentrated requests give 66667, each derived independently from processing rates and integer capacity. Two wrong programs exit normally and are rejected by the official cases.
